section.title: Teach Me Your Way, O Lord
section.sectionRationale: The only psalm of David set among the Korah and Asaph collections of Book III, this personal prayer of a poor and needy servant appeals to God's mercy, uniqueness, and steadfast love, asking for an undivided heart, a request answered fully in the perfect, single-hearted devotion of Christ.
section.thesis: David, poor and needy yet trusting, appeals to the LORD's kindness, forgiveness, and steadfast love, asking to be taught God's way and given an undivided heart, a prayer answered in Christ, who both perfectly walked in the Father's way and unites divided hearts to Himself.
section.frameNote: Five movements: a personal plea from need, verses 1-5; confidence in God's readiness to answer, verses 6-7; praise for God's incomparable greatness, verses 8-10; a prayer for an undivided heart, verses 11-13; and a cry for help against enemies, verses 14-17.

verses.text: Incline Your ear, O LORD, and answer me, for I am poor and needy.
Preserve my soul, for I am godly. You are my God; save Your servant who trusts in You.
Be merciful to me, O Lord, for I call to You all day long.
Bring joy to Your servant, for to You, O Lord, I lift up my soul.
For You, O Lord, are kind and forgiving, rich in {{chesed|loving devotion}} to all who call on You.

units.label: Confidence That God Answers
units.note: trust in God's readiness to hear

verses.text: Hear my prayer, O LORD, and attend to my plea for mercy.
In the day of my distress I call on You, because You answer me.
O Lord, there is none like You among the gods, nor any works like Yours.
All the nations You have made will come and bow before You, O Lord, and they will glorify Your name.
For You are great and perform wonders; You alone are God.
Teach me Your way, O LORD, that I may walk in Your truth. Give me an {{yachad|undivided}} heart, that I may fear Your name.
I will praise You, O Lord my God, with all my heart; I will glorify Your name forever.
For great is Your loving devotion to me; You have delivered me from the depths of {{sheol|Sheol}}.
The arrogant rise against me, O God; a band of ruthless men seeks my life; they have no regard for You.
But You, O Lord, are a {{rachum|compassionate}} and gracious God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness.
Turn to me and have mercy; grant Your strength to Your servant; save the son of Your maidservant.
Show me a sign of Your goodness, that my enemies may see and be ashamed; for You, O LORD, have helped me and comforted me.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast, covenant love. David grounds his confidence in prayer not on his own merit but on the character of a God who is rich in this loyal love toward all who call on Him.

yachad.gloss: United, joined together, as one. David's prayer for an undivided heart asks that every competing loyalty be joined into a single, wholehearted devotion to God's name.

sheol.gloss: The realm of the dead, the grave. David praises God for a deliverance so great that it reached even to the brink of death itself.

rachum.gloss: Compassionate, full of tender mercy. This word, drawn from God's self-revelation to Moses, describes the deep, parental mercy David appeals to when facing ruthless enemies.

basic.context: David, poor and needy and hunted by ruthless enemies, prays this deeply personal psalm. He appeals again and again to God's mercy and steadfast love, praises God's incomparable greatness among all the nations, and asks for a heart that is wholly, undividedly devoted to God alone.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm describes David's own crisis, yet its pattern of humble appeal, praise for God's uniqueness, and prayer for an undivided heart offers a lasting model for anyone approaching God from a place of need.
basic.originalLanguages: David appeals to God's chesed, steadfast love, verse 5, and asks for a yachad, undivided or united, heart, verse 11. He praises the rachum, compassionate, God who has delivered him from the depths of sheol, the realm of the dead, verse 13.
basic.typology: David's plea for an undivided heart wholly devoted to God's name anticipates the perfectly single-hearted obedience of Christ, who always did what was pleasing to the Father, and who unites divided, wandering hearts to Himself.
basic.christ: David's deliverance from the depths of Sheol, verse 13, foreshadows the greater deliverance from death accomplished in Christ's resurrection, Acts 2:24-31. And the nations bowing before the LORD, verse 9, anticipates every tribe and tongue worshiping before the Lamb, Revelation 15:4.
basic.god: God is shown as kind, forgiving, rich in loving devotion, incomparably great among all so-called gods, compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, and utterly faithful, a God who answers in the day of distress.
basic.crossReferences: Revelation 15:4 echoes the nations coming to worship the LORD. Acts 2:24-31 shows resurrection life triumphing over Sheol, ultimately in Christ. Philippians 2:9-11 pictures every knee bowing to Jesus, fulfilling verse 9's vision.
basic.oneStory: David's plea for an undivided heart and his confidence in the God who alone is God, who forgives, delivers from death, and answers prayer, finds its fullest answer in Christ, whose single-hearted obedience to the Father secures for us the very undivided devotion David longed for.

context.literary:
Psalm 86 is built like a mosaic. Many lines have a close relative elsewhere in Scripture, and the psalmist seems to have gathered the prayers of his people into one cry of his own. The shape is a rough chiasm around the praise of verses 8 to 10. The opening plea, verses 1 to 7, is matched by the closing plea, verses 14 to 17; both begin with the speaker's need and both end with a confession that God answers or has helped. At the hinge sit the two requests of verse 11, to be taught and to be united, framed on either side by the exaltation of God's name in verses 9 to 10 and verse 12.

Watch the small repeated words. The title 'Lord' in its gentle form, Adonai, rings through the psalm, and the speaker calls himself 'Your servant' in verses 2, 4 and 16 and, at the very end, 'the son of Your maidservant.' The logic of the psalm is a string of 'for' clauses: hear me, for I am poor; be merciful, for I call; bring joy, for I lift up my soul; You are kind, for You answer. Each request carries its own reason, and the reasons are nearly all about God rather than about the petitioner.

The genre is an individual lament, but unusually quiet. There is an enemy, verse 14, yet he appears only near the end, and most of the psalm is spent not on him but on who God is. The centre of gravity is the great confession of verse 15, which borrows the words God spoke to Moses.
context.historical:
The heading names David, and the psalm's mixture of royal and personal notes fits a man who was both anointed and hunted. The phrase 'poor and needy' is David's own signature in prayer, appearing also in Psalm 40:17 and Psalm 70:5, and it is a striking thing for a king to say. It describes his standing before God, not his bank balance. The 'band of ruthless men' of verse 14 recalls Saul's pursuit, or later uprisings against his rule, and the phrase 'they have no regard for You' marks the enemy as opposed to God as much as to David.

The psalm also shows how much of Israel's worship was built from remembered words. The description of God in verse 15 is the self-revelation given at Sinai in Exodus 34:6, recited again and again by later generations. The claim that none among the gods is like the LORD, verse 8, recalls the song at the sea, Exodus 15:11. A praying Israelite in the time of the monarchy would have heard the psalm as a web of familiar phrases, and taken comfort from that familiarity.

The description 'son of Your maidservant,' verse 16, names a servant born in the household, a person whose belonging is settled from birth. The same phrase appears in Psalm 116:16. It is a humble claim of status: the speaker is a house servant with a household's claim on its master's protection. The mention of the nations bowing, verse 9, reflects the Davidic age, when Israel's king was already drawing neighbouring peoples into the orbit of Israel's God.
context.canonical:
Psalm 86 is the only psalm of David in Book III, which otherwise belongs to Asaph and the sons of Korah. It stands among laments over a fallen temple and a shaken promise, Psalms 74, 79 and 89, like a single steady lamp. Its neighbours are anxious about the nation; this psalm is about one servant who still knows his Master's character. Right after it comes Psalm 87, where Zion is given citizens from every people, and that placement is not accidental, for verse 9 has already promised that all the nations God made will come and bow.

The psalm looks backward to the Torah in two places, verse 8 to Exodus 15:11 and verse 15 to Exodus 34:6, and its prayer to be taught and to walk in truth echoes Psalm 25:4 to 5 and Psalm 27:11. It looks forward to the promise that God would give His people 'one heart and one way,' Jeremiah 32:39, and to the new heart of Ezekiel 11:19. The prophets answer verse 11 in the form of a promise: what David begged for, God pledges to do in the new covenant.

In the New Testament the vision of verse 9 is taken up in Revelation 15:4, where the nations come and worship before God, and in Philippians 2:9 to 11, where every knee bows to Jesus. James treats the divided heart as a spiritual disease, calling the double minded man unstable, James 1:8, and calls believers to purify their hearts, James 4:8. Psalm 86 gives the prayer; the New Testament shows the answer.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David meant his hearers to learn how to pray when they are at the end of their resources, and the lesson is built into the order of the psalm. He begins with need, but he does not stay there. He reminds himself of God's character before he asks for anything large. That order is deliberate: a petition that springs from who God is stands on firmer ground than one that springs only from how bad things are.

He also meant to show what the deepest request of a believer is. After asking for rescue he asks to be taught, and after being taught he asks to be united, so that he might fear the name rather than merely survive. Safety from enemies matters to him, but being whole before God matters more. A king who could ask for anything asks for a single heart.

A further aim is to hold together two things that easily come apart: boldness and humility. He calls himself poor and needy and yet dares to say 'You are my God' and 'You will answer.' The plain message to Israel is that a humble servant is not a timid one, and that a person with no claim of his own may lean with full weight on the promises God has made about Himself.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records David's own prayer in a particular crisis. It does not promise every reader that enemies will be put to shame on a schedule, and verse 17, asking for a sign that enemies may see and be ashamed, is a request, not a guarantee. The psalm's own petitions remain open prayers, and the answer in verse 13 describes what God had already done for David, not what He will do for everyone in the same way.

What carries forward is the shape of the prayer. Believers are invited to appeal to God's revealed character, verses 5 and 15, to ask for teaching before asking for ease, verse 11, and to praise in the middle of trouble, verse 12. The claim 'I am godly' in verse 2 should not be read as boasting. The word describes one who belongs to God's covenant love and lives in response to it, not one who has earned a hearing. Nor does the prayer license a hard heart toward enemies; the psalmist leaves their shaming in God's hands.

debates.question: When the psalmist says 'I am godly' in verse 2, is this a claim of personal righteousness that sits oddly with his plea for mercy?

views.label: A claim of covenant loyalty, not merit
views.case: The word is from the same root as the covenant love of verse 5. It describes one who is a recipient and practitioner of loyal love, and the request that follows, 'be merciful to me,' verse 3, shows that he stands on mercy. David says the same elsewhere, pleading innocence against his enemies while confessing sin before God, as in Psalm 51.

views.label: A claim of relative innocence against his accusers
views.case: In the face of enemies who have no regard for God, verse 14, the psalmist contrasts himself with them. He is not claiming sinlessness but faithfulness in the matter at hand, as Job does when he refuses to give up his integrity before his friends.

debates.bearing: On either reading the plea rests on God's kindness in verse 5, not on the speaker's record. The psalm teaches believers to be honest about their loyalty without turning it into a bargaining chip.

debates.question: Does the nations' coming in verse 9 describe a hope within Israel's history or the end of the age?

views.label: A hope for the spread of Israel's witness within history
views.case: Davidic psalms regularly picture neighbouring nations turning to the LORD through what He has done for His king, Psalm 18:43 to 49 being a clear example. On this reading verse 9 is a confident forecast of the widening reach of David's God.

views.label: An end-time vision of all nations worshipping
views.case: The words 'all the nations You have made' seem to reach every people. The New Testament takes the verse this way, finding its completion when the nations worship before God, Revelation 15:4, and every knee bows to Jesus, Philippians 2:10 to 11.

debates.bearing: The two readings are not rivals. The verse states a hope that begins in David's day and finds its full scope in Christ. It warns believers against treating the gospel as a private possession.

study.originalLanguages:
Four words and phrases reward a slower look, beyond the ones the basic text names.

The first is the pair 'poor and needy' in verse 1, ani and evyon. Ani describes a person bowed low, afflicted and dependent, and evyon describes one who is in want and must ask. Together they are David's favourite self description in prayer, Psalm 40:17, Psalm 70:5 and Psalm 109:22. They are not a confession of poverty in money but of having nothing to bring. The same two words in Deuteronomy 15:11 and Psalm 72:12 to 13 describe those the king and God are pledged to defend, so the psalmist is placing himself among the people God has promised to help.

The second is the verb behind 'Give me an undivided heart' in verse 11. The BSB supplies the adjective 'undivided,' but the Hebrew is a request that God unite, or bring together, the heart, using the same root that means 'together' in Hebrew. The picture is a heart in pieces, pulled in several directions by fear, desire and loyalty, asking for one act of gathering. Psalm 12:2 describes the opposite, people who speak 'with a heart and a heart,' that is, a double heart. James takes up the same idea in Greek with the word dipsuchos, double minded, James 1:8.

The third is the phrase 'Incline Your ear' in verse 1, a figure from a face bending down to hear a quiet voice. It is used again in Psalm 88:2, in the next psalm but one. The verb 'answer' that follows is the same one used in verse 7, 'You answer me,' so that the request of verse 1 becomes the testimony of verse 7.

The fourth is the verb that stands behind 'I lift up my soul' in verse 4. The soul, nephesh, is the whole self in its need, and to lift it is to hand over the entire person, as in Psalm 25:1. The 'joy' the psalmist asks for in the same verse is not an emotion to be manufactured but a gift to be received from the God to whom he has lifted himself.

Finally the word for 'sign' in verse 17, ot, is the word used of the signs given to Moses and of the sign of the covenant. The psalmist is not asking for a spectacle but for a visible mark of God's goodness toward him that his enemies cannot miss. Translators render the word plainly, but it carries the weight of a covenant pledge made visible.

typology.type: The poor and needy servant, Psalm 86:1, 16
typology.fulfillment: David prays as one with no claim except God's kindness, and he ends as 'the son of Your maidservant,' a servant born in the house. The pattern finds its fullest form in Christ, who was anointed to preach good news to the poor, Luke 4:18, and who, though rich, became poor for our sake, 2 Corinthians 8:9. David is poor by circumstance; Jesus chose poverty. The type falls short because David needed rescue himself, while Christ, the faithful Servant, Philippians 2:7, brings the rescue.

typology.type: The prayer to be taught God's way, Psalm 86:11
typology.fulfillment: David asks to learn God's way and walk in His truth. Jesus fulfils this as the Son who learned obedience through what He suffered, Hebrews 5:8, and who could say 'I always do what pleases Him,' John 8:29. He is the way and the truth, John 14:6, so that the prayer of the psalm finds its answer in a person to follow. The correspondence is between a petitioner and a perfect Son; the difference is that Jesus never needed his heart to be united, for it was never divided.

typology.type: The nations bowing to the LORD, Psalm 86:9
typology.fulfillment: David's hope that all the nations will come and bow is the seed of the vision that fills Revelation, where the nations sing the song of the Lamb and say 'all nations will come and worship before You,' Revelation 15:4. Jesus said that when He was lifted up He would draw all people to Himself, John 12:32, and Paul describes the day when every knee bows at His name, Philippians 2:10. The type is partial in David's day, since only a few neighbours came; it is universal in Christ, though its full display still waits for the last day.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first by the pattern of a servant in need of deliverance. David speaks of depths of Sheol and of a band of ruthless men seeking his life, verses 13 and 14. In the Gospels the same combination appears in the days before the cross. A crowd with swords and clubs comes out against Jesus in the garden, Matthew 26:55, and the authorities plot to have Him put to death. Hebrews says that Jesus 'offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death,' Hebrews 5:7, and adds that He was heard because of His reverent submission. The servant who pleaded 'Turn to me and have mercy' in Psalm 86 is shadowed by the greater Servant who prayed the same kind of prayer at Gethsemane.

It leads to Christ by the request of verse 11. David asked to be taught, to walk in truth, and to fear the name with an undivided heart. Jesus is the one who actually lived that life. He spoke of doing the Father's will as His food, John 4:34, of doing nothing on His own, John 5:30, and of always doing what pleases the Father, John 8:29. On the night of His arrest He prayed that His followers might be one, John 17:11 and 21, which is the prayer of Psalm 86:11 lifted to a larger scale, a prayer for the uniting of a scattered people. The Spirit who is given through Him is the answer to the gathered heart that Jeremiah and Ezekiel promise, Ezekiel 11:19 to 20.

It leads to Christ by the confession of verse 13, 'You have delivered me from the depths of Sheol.' David received a rescue from the edge of the grave. Peter, preaching at Pentecost, shows that the ultimate rescue from death belongs to David's Son, who was not abandoned to the grave, Acts 2:27 to 31. What David tasted in part, Christ received in full when God raised Him.

And it leads to Christ through the nations. Verses 9 and 12 pledge that the nations will glorify God's name, and the New Testament shows the name Jesus is given 'the name that is above every name,' Philippians 2:9. Care is needed. Not every line of the psalm is spoken in Jesus' voice; verse 2 and verse 4 describe a petitioner whose trust grows in the telling, and the New Testament nowhere quotes the psalm as the words of Christ. The honest link is that Christ completes what the psalm asks for, a servant who is heard, a heart made single, and a world brought to bow.
study.god:
The psalm teaches the doctrine of God by giving the reasons behind its prayers. He is kind and forgiving, verse 5. He is great and works wonders, verse 10, and He alone is God. He is compassionate, gracious, slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness, verse 15, which is the credal centre of the Old Testament, given to Moses after Israel's worship of the golden calf, Exodus 34:6. The psalmist does not choose these attributes to suit himself. He cites what God has said of Himself.

The psalm holds together two things that people find hard to hold together: the uniqueness of God and His nearness. Verses 8 and 10 confess that none among the gods is like Him and that He alone is God. Verses 1 and 6 picture Him bending to hear the faint prayer of one poor man. The God who rules the nations is the God who inclines His ear. This is why prayer in Israel could be both bold and humble, and it is a pattern for ours.

The psalm also shows that God is the teacher of His people. The request in verse 11 assumes that a believer cannot find the way by himself; God must instruct, and God must also unite the heart that has been divided. The work of making a person single hearted is God's work, which is why the prayer is a prayer and not a resolution. In the new covenant He promises to do just this, 'I will give them one heart and one way,' Jeremiah 32:39.

The psalm shows God as sovereign over the day of distress. Verse 7 says 'You answer me,' and verse 17 says 'You have helped me and comforted me.' Notice that the help arrives alongside the trouble, not always after it; the enemies are still present in verse 14. Worship here is not reserved for after deliverance. The psalm teaches believers to glorify His name with all the heart, verse 12, while the danger is still near, because God's character does not change when circumstances do.

Finally, the God of this psalm has a claim on all the nations. The nations 'You have made,' verse 9, belong to Him by creation, and they will one day acknowledge it. His mercy is not a tribal possession. This shapes worship: we come as beggars to a King whose kindness is meant for the whole world.

crossReferences.note: The words God spoke to Moses as He passed before him: compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness. Psalm 86:15 repeats them nearly word for word, turning God's self-description into the ground of a personal plea. The psalmist treats what God has said of Himself as binding on God's own mercy.

The song at the sea asks who is like the LORD among the gods. Psalm 86:8 answers in the same terms, so that the psalmist's confession of God's incomparability echoes the first great act of redemption. The One who freed Israel from Egypt is the One who hears a single servant.

David says elsewhere that he is poor and needy and asks the Lord to think of him. The same self-description as Psalm 86:1 shows that it is his habitual stance in prayer, and that the psalm is the voice of a man who knew his dependence well.

A prayer to be shown God's ways and led in His truth, close to verse 11. Both psalms treat guidance as something God must give, and both rest the request on God's goodness. Setting the two side by side shows how David's prayers form a single school.

Another believer who calls himself the son of God's maidservant, in a psalm of thanks for deliverance from death. The phrase in Psalm 86:16 is the same, and the pairing suggests a household image: a servant born into the master's house has a claim on his protection.

God promises to give His people one heart and one way. It is the answer, in covenant language, to the request of Psalm 86:11. What David prayed for as a personal gift, God pledges to do for the whole people in the new covenant.

James describes a double minded man as unstable in all his ways. The word is the New Testament counterpart to the divided heart of Psalm 86:11. James applies the warning to prayer, which fits the psalm: the undivided heart is what makes prayer steady.
The nations come and worship before God and glorify His name, in words that echo Psalm 86:9 and 12. The vision of the psalm is seen fulfilled in heaven, sung as the song of Moses and the Lamb.
Jesus offered prayers with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and was heard. It shows the greater Servant praying the kind of prayer Psalm 86 gives, and being answered.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 86 sits in the middle of the Bible's long story about a people who need to be taught, united and rescued. It answers a question raised earlier in the Psalter: what does a person do when God's promises seem far and his enemies near? David's answer is to pray with God's own words, to ask to be taught, and to ask for a heart that is whole.

Looking back, the psalm draws on creation and Exodus. The nations 'You have made,' verse 9, echo the Genesis truth that God made all peoples from one, and the word of God to Abraham that through his line all nations would be blessed, Genesis 12:3. The compassion of verse 15 recalls the moment after the golden calf when God proclaimed His own name to Moses. In the story of the fall, human hearts were split from God and from one another, Genesis 3:8; Psalm 86:11 is the prayer of a person who feels that split and asks God to heal it.

Looking forward, the psalm prepares for the new covenant. The prophets promise the gift David begged for: God will give His people one heart and put His Spirit within them, Ezekiel 11:19 and 36:26. The psalm prepares for Christ, who lived the undivided life, prayed in the night of His distress, and was delivered from death. It prepares for the gathering of the nations, which Paul describes as the mystery now revealed, that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, Ephesians 3:6.

The story ends where the psalm's verse 9 ends. In Revelation the nations God made come and worship, Revelation 15:4, and the kings of the earth bring their glory into the city, Revelation 21:24. The heart that was split in Eden is finally made single, and the name David promised to glorify forever is glorified in a new creation. A prayer of one poor man is a small part of that great movement, and it belongs to it fully.

sermon.title: The Lord Is Great and Does Wondrous Things
sermon.why: Preaching directly from Psalm 86:8-10, Piper draws out the psalm's confession that the LORD alone is God among all the nations, grounding worship and prayer in God's incomparable greatness, the very heart of this psalm's praise.

quiz.q: How does David describe himself as he begins his prayer in verses 1-2?

options.text: Poor and needy, yet godly and trusting in God.
options.note: David's opening plea rests on his neediness and his trust, not on his own strength.

options.text: Wealthy and self-sufficient.
options.note: David describes himself as poor and needy, the opposite of self-sufficient.

options.text: A king with no enemies.
options.note: The psalm later reveals ruthless enemies seeking his life; he is not without opposition.

options.text: A servant who trusts in God.
options.note: This is true, verse 2, and closely related, though the fuller self-description in verses 1-2 is poor, needy, and godly.

quiz.q: What does David declare about God in verse 10?

options.text: You are great and perform wonders; You alone are God.
options.note: Verse 10 is the psalm's clear declaration of God's sole and supreme divinity.

options.text: There are many gods equal to the LORD.
options.note: The psalm insists there is none like the LORD and that He alone is God.

options.text: God is distant and uninvolved.
options.note: The psalm portrays an involved God who answers prayer and performs wonders.

options.text: All the nations will one day bow and glorify His name.
options.note: This truth appears in verse 9, closely related, though verse 10 specifically declares God's sole and supreme deity: You alone are God.

quiz.q: What does David ask for in verse 11?

options.text: To be taught God's way and given an undivided heart to fear His name.
options.note: Verse 11 is David's central prayer for wholehearted, singular devotion to God.

options.text: To be given more wealth and possessions.
options.note: David's request is for spiritual singleness of heart, not material gain.

options.text: To be freed from ever praying again.
options.note: The psalm models ongoing prayer, not its cessation.

options.text: To have his soul preserved as God's servant.
options.note: This is true and part of David's earlier plea, verse 2, though verse 11 specifically prays for being taught God's way and given an undivided heart.

quiz.q: What deliverance does David celebrate in verse 13?

options.text: Being delivered from the depths of Sheol because of God's great loving devotion.
options.note: Verse 13 praises God's steadfast love for a deliverance reaching even to the brink of death.

options.text: Victory in a specific military battle.
options.note: The verse speaks of deliverance from Sheol, not a named battle.

options.text: Being rescued from a life-threatening danger.
options.note: This is a fair general description, though the verse specifically names deliverance from the depths of Sheol, the realm of the dead.

options.text: Nothing; the verse describes ongoing suffering.
options.note: The verse is a clear declaration of past deliverance, not ongoing suffering.

quiz.q: How does David's prayer for an undivided heart point toward Christ?

options.text: It anticipates Christ's perfectly single-hearted devotion to the Father, who unites divided hearts to Himself.
options.note: Jesus always did what pleased the Father, John 8:29, and He alone can give His people the undivided heart David asked for.

options.text: It has no connection to the New Testament.
options.note: The theme of wholehearted devotion runs directly into Christ's own perfect obedience.

options.text: It predicts a specific future king of Israel unrelated to Jesus.
options.note: The psalm's language of undivided devotion to God finds its fulfillment in Christ, not merely a future earthly king.

options.text: It shows the deep human longing for wholehearted devotion to God.
options.note: This is true as far as it goes, but the prayer's answer is found not merely in longing but in Christ's own perfect obedience and His gift of a new heart to His people.

questions: David repeatedly appeals to God's character rather than his own merit. When you pray, are you tempted to rely on your own worthiness rather than on God's steadfast love?
Verse 11 prays for an undivided heart. What competing loyalties or divided affections most threaten your wholehearted devotion to God right now?
David praises God's incomparable greatness even while surrounded by ruthless enemies. How does remembering who God is change the way you face opposition or hardship?
David's deliverance from Sheol points forward to Christ's resurrection victory over death. How does the assurance of that greater deliverance shape your hope today?
Verse 17 asks for a visible sign of God's goodness so that enemies would be ashamed. Where in your life could you ask God for evidence of His goodness that would strengthen your witness to others?

translationNotes.note: Godly renders a Hebrew word meaning one who is faithful or the recipient of God's covenant loyalty, not a claim of sinless perfection.
Undivided heart translates a phrase meaning literally a heart made one, picturing every scattered loyalty gathered into a single devotion to God.
Son of Your maidservant is a humble self-description meaning one born into a household devoted to serving God from birth.
